items.readable_text:
Content:
Consider the following integral:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{x^2+2x+5}\, \textrm{d}x]

Content:
This integral doesn't resemble any of the standard integrals we have encountered so far.

Content:
However, notice that we can complete the square in the denominator as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x^{2} + 2x + 5|= x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 1 ⋅ x + 5; = x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 1 ⋅ x + (1^{2} − 1^{2}) + 5; = (x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 1 ⋅ x + 1^{2}) − 1^{2} + 5; = (x + 1)^{2} + 4]

Content:
If we plug the above into our integral and collect a factor of [MATH: {\color{red}{4}}], we get
[MATH: ∫(1)/(x^{2} + 2x + 5)dx|= ∫(1)/((x + 1)^{2} + 4)dx; = ∫(1)/(4[(x + 1)^{2}/4 + 1])dx; = (1)/(4)∫(1)/((x + 1)^{2}/4 + 1)dx; = (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 + (x + 1)^{2}/4)dx; = (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 + ((x + 1)/2)^{2})dx.]

Content:
Notice that this now resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u = \arctan u + C]

Content:
The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac{x+1}{2}\right).]

Content:
So, let's perform the substitution
[MATH: u=\dfrac{x+1}{2}.]

Content:
Differentiating, we get
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Content:
Finally, we write the integral in terms of [MATH: u,] and evaluate:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(x^{2} + 2x + 5)dx|= (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 + ((x + 1)/2)^{2})dx; = (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 + u^{2}) ⋅ 2du; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 + u^{2})du; = (1)/(2)\arctan u + C; = (1)/(2)\arctan ((x + 1)/(2)) + C]

Content:
And we're done!

Let's rewrite our integral as follows: [MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(36 − (3x − 2)^{2}))dx|= ∫(1)/(sqrt(36(1 − (3x − 2)^{2}/36)))dx; = ∫(1)/(sqrt(36) ⋅ sqrt(1 − (3x − 2)^{2}/36))dx; = ∫(1)/(6sqrt(1 − (3x − 2)^{2}/36))dx; = (1)/(6)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − (3x − 2)^{2}/36))dx; = (1)/(6)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − ((3x − 2)/6)^{2}))dx]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine: [MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u + C]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac{3x-2}{6}\right).]

So, let's perform the substitution [MATH: u=\dfrac{3x-2}{6}.]

Differentiating, we get [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of [MATH: u,] and evaluate:

[MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(36 − (3x − 2)^{2}))dx|= (1)/(6)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − ((3x − 2)/6)^{2}))dx; = (1)/(6)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − u^{2})) ⋅ 2du; = (1)/(3)\arcsin u + C; = (1)/(3)\arcsin ((3x − 2)/(6)) + C]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square in the denominator: [MATH: \eqalign{ x^2-2x + 3 & = x^2 - 2 \cdot x+ (1^2 - 1^2) + 3 \[3pt] & = (x^2 - 2 \cdot x+ 1^2) - 1 + 3 \[3pt] & = (x-1)^2+2 }]

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get [MATH: ∫(1)/(x^{2} − 2x + 3)dx|= ∫(1)/((x − 1)^{2} + 2)dx; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 + ((x − 1)/sqrt(2))^{2})dx.]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent: [MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u = \arctan u + C.]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac{x-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right).]

So, let's perform the substitution

[MATH: u=\dfrac{x-1}{\sqrt{2}}.] Differentiating, we get [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \sqrt{2}\,\textrm{d}u.]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of [MATH: u,] and evaluate:

[MATH: ∫(1)/(x^{2} − 2x + 3)dx|= (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 + ((x − 1)/sqrt(2))^{2})dx; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 + u^{2}) ⋅ sqrt(2)du; = (sqrt(2))/(2)∫(1)/(1 + u^{2})du; = (sqrt(2))/(2)\arctan u + C; = (sqrt(2))/(2)\arctan ((x − 1)/(sqrt(2))) + C]

items.title: Computing an Arcsine Integral by Completing the Square

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: [MATH: 4x − 4x^{2}|= − (4x^{2} − 4x); = − ((2x)^{2} − 2 ⋅ 2x + 1 − 1); = − ((2x − 1)^{2} − 1); = 1 − (2x − 1)^{2}]

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get [MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(4x − 4x^{2}))dx|= ∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − (2x − 1)^{2}))dx.]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:

[MATH: \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u+C]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: (2x - 1).]

So, let's perform the substitution

[MATH: u =2x - 1.] Differentiating, we get

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \dfrac12\textrm{d}u.]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of [MATH: u,] and evaluate:

[MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(4x − 4x^{2}))dx|= ∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − (2x − 1)^{2}))dx; = ∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − u^{2})) ⋅ (1)/(2)du; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − u^{2}))du; = (1)/(2)\arcsin u + C; = (1)/(2)\arcsin (2x − 1) + C.]

items.title: Computing an Arcsecant Integral by Completing the Square

sections.normalized_html:
First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root: [MATH: \eqalign{ x^2-2x&= x^2 -2x +(1-1)\[3pt] &= (x^2 -2x +1)-1\[3pt] &= (x-1)^2-1 }]

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get [MATH: \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{x^2-2x}}\, \textrm{d}x = \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{(x-1)^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}x.]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

[MATH: \int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \, \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec} \, u +C]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: x-1.]

So, let's perform the substitution [MATH: u=x-1.] Differentiating, we get [MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.]

Let's use the table below to change the limits from [MATH: x] to [MATH: u.]

[MATH: x]

[MATH: 1+\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}]

[MATH: 3]

[MATH: u]

[MATH: \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}]

[MATH: 2]

Therefore,

[MATH: \eqalign{ \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3} \dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{x^2-2x}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{1+2/\sqrt{3}}^{3}\dfrac{1}{|x-1|\sqrt{(x-1)^2-1}}\,\textrm{d}x \[5pt] &=\int_{2/\sqrt{3}}^{2} \dfrac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u\[5pt] &= \textrm{arcsec}\, {u}\Big|_{2/\sqrt{3}}^{2}\[5pt] &= \textrm{arcsec} \left(2\right) - \textrm{arcsec}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \right)\[5pt] &=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\pi}{6}. }]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the following integral:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{x^2+2x+5}\, \textrm{d}x]

Content:
This integral doesn't resemble any of the standard integrals we have encountered so far.

Content:
However, notice that we can complete the square in the denominator as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x^{2} + 2x + 5|= x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 1 ⋅ x + 5; = x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 1 ⋅ x + (1^{2} − 1^{2}) + 5; = (x^{2} + 2 ⋅ 1 ⋅ x + 1^{2}) − 1^{2} + 5; = (x + 1)^{2} + 4]

Content:
If we plug the above into our integral and collect a factor of [MATH: {\color{red}{4}}], we get
[MATH: ∫(1)/(x^{2} + 2x + 5)dx|= ∫(1)/((x + 1)^{2} + 4)dx; = ∫(1)/(4[(x + 1)^{2}/4 + 1])dx; = (1)/(4)∫(1)/((x + 1)^{2}/4 + 1)dx; = (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 + (x + 1)^{2}/4)dx; = (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 + ((x + 1)/2)^{2})dx.]

Content:
Notice that this now resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u = \arctan u + C]

Content:
The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac{x+1}{2}\right).]

Content:
So, let's perform the substitution
[MATH: u=\dfrac{x+1}{2}.]

Content:
Differentiating, we get
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Content:
Finally, we write the integral in terms of [MATH: u,] and evaluate:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(x^{2} + 2x + 5)dx|= (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 + ((x + 1)/2)^{2})dx; = (1)/(4)∫(1)/(1 + u^{2}) ⋅ 2du; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 + u^{2})du; = (1)/(2)\arctan u + C; = (1)/(2)\arctan ((x + 1)/(2)) + C]

Content:
And we're done!

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating Inverse Trigonometric Function Integrals Using Substitution

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{36 -(3x - 2)^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:
[MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(36 − (3x − 2)^{2}))dx|= ∫(1)/(sqrt(36(1 − (3x − 2)^{2}/36)))dx; = ∫(1)/(sqrt(36) ⋅ sqrt(1 − (3x − 2)^{2}/36))dx; = ∫(1)/(6sqrt(1 − (3x − 2)^{2}/36))dx; = (1)/(6)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − (3x − 2)^{2}/36))dx; = (1)/(6)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − ((3x − 2)/6)^{2}))dx]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u + C]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac{3x-2}{6}\right).]

So, let's perform the substitution
[MATH: u=\dfrac{3x-2}{6}.]

Differentiating, we get
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of [MATH: u,] and evaluate:

[MATH: ∫(1)/(sqrt(36 − (3x − 2)^{2}))dx|= (1)/(6)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − ((3x − 2)/6)^{2}))dx; = (1)/(6)∫(1)/(sqrt(1 − u^{2})) ⋅ 2du; = (1)/(3)\arcsin u + C; = (1)/(3)\arcsin ((3x − 2)/(6)) + C]

Item 6 — Example: Computing an Arctangent Integral by Completing the Square

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{x^2-2x + 3}\, \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we complete the square in the denominator:
[MATH: \eqalign{
x^2-2x + 3
& = x^2 - 2 \cdot x+ (1^2 - 1^2) + 3 \[3pt]
& = (x^2 - 2 \cdot x+ 1^2) - 1 + 3 \[3pt]
& = (x-1)^2+2
}]

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get
[MATH: ∫(1)/(x^{2} − 2x + 3)dx|= ∫(1)/((x − 1)^{2} + 2)dx; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 + ((x − 1)/sqrt(2))^{2})dx.]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent:
[MATH: \int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u
=
\arctan u + C.]

The only difference is that instead of [MATH: u] as the variable, we have [MATH: \left(\dfrac{x-1}{\sqrt{2}}\right).]

So, let's perform the substitution

[MATH: u=\dfrac{x-1}{\sqrt{2}}.]
Differentiating, we get
[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \sqrt{2}\,\textrm{d}u.]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of [MATH: u,] and evaluate:

[MATH: ∫(1)/(x^{2} − 2x + 3)dx|= (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 + ((x − 1)/sqrt(2))^{2})dx; = (1)/(2)∫(1)/(1 + u^{2}) ⋅ sqrt(2)du; = (sqrt(2))/(2)∫(1)/(1 + u^{2})du; = (sqrt(2))/(2)\arctan u + C; = (sqrt(2))/(2)\arctan ((x − 1)/(sqrt(2))) + C]
